anchors.fact: Harry McElhone, a Scot from Dundee who left school at fourteen, owned and ran Harry's New York Bar in Paris from 1923 until his death in 1958. (F1)
anchors.meaning: One address and one odd identity, for a whole working life.

anchors.fact: He advertised the bar's address, 5 rue Daunou, in Paris's American newspapers spelled out as "Sank Roo Doe Noo". (F3)
anchors.meaning: A made-up spelling, used until it became how people said it. **Reading:** "so an American could say it". Never the taxi (*Worth the Trip*). The spelling is still on a later IBF booklet's cover (F22).

anchors.fact: Among the paper jokes Oxford lists are "self-deprecating" postcards. (F2)
anchors.meaning: He was the joke first. "First" is **our reading**: signpost it or drop it.

anchors.fact: As his bar's 1927 book tells it: in autumn 1924 the columnist O. O. McIntyre wrote a "mournful" magazine piece calling Paris's regulars "barflies". A Montmartre club man then advertised his Christmas Eve takings for the "needy barflies", and Harry answered with an advert calling a meeting. Around Christmas 1924, the International Bar Flies, Trap 1, was organised at his bar. (F5; C1)
anchors.meaning: He took up someone else's joke and made it real, then kept it. The joke on the page is **the club man's advert**, not McIntyre's piece, which the book calls mournful. The meeting gets one clause (Wren). **Label:** "the way his own book tells it". **Never** "co-founded with McIntyre" (C1) or "Harry coined barfly" (L5). "Barflies" is glossed once, kindly (Wren): the regulars who never seem to leave.

anchors.fact: The presidency was "foisted upon" McIntyre as the "unconscious inspirer", as "Big Blue Bottlefly". The book lists Harry as vice-president, "Little Blue Bottlefly". (F6)
McIntyre's middle name really was Odd: Oscar Odd McIntyre (Library of Congress). Friends called him Odd. (F10)
anchors.meaning: One plain clause, owned as a coincidence. Never explain the name.

anchors.fact: The book prints the society's emblem, a housefly on a sugar lump lettered "I.B.F." (printed p. 94). (F17)
anchors.meaning: The fly is the society's own image. **No sugar lumps with dead flies in guest text** (Wren). The coffee beans are sambuca's custom (see spark).

anchors.fact: By 1927: over five thousand members and branches called "traps" all over the world, and it kept growing for years (Oxford). The book's list starts at Trap 1, his bar, and includes a Trap 17 in Shanghai. Its chapter has members greeting each other "in Shanghai or Liverpool, Madrid or Pittsburg". (F4, F7, F20)
anchors.meaning: The daft thing became part of the world. Reading v2: "members, from Shanghai to Pittsburgh, and its branches were called traps". That's the chapter's own range for the members (p. 85). Pittsburgh isn't on the list of traps (F20), so never "traps from… Pittsburgh". No rules quoted (Wren).

anchors.fact: In 1940, with German troops closing in, he locked his papers in a safe, buried it outside Paris and left for London. After the war he came back and "picked up where he left off", running the bar until his death. (F14)
anchors.meaning: The serious stretch came, the joke was put somewhere safe, and he came back. **Scope:** Oxford's line is about the *bar*. No son, no bomb, no Café de Paris (Wren).

anchors.fact: A later IBF membership booklet (a dealer dates it 1953) lists "President: Exalted Blue Bottle Fly Harry Mc Elhone", with three more McElhones on its committee, and Harry signs its membership card as President. (F22)
anchors.meaning: The flies came back too, and he'd gone from "Little" to "Exalted" ("He'd been promoted": our joke, true of the two listed titles). "A later booklet", with no date (1953 is the dealer's). Its contents are post-1934, and its place after the war sentence rests on the dealer's date. Never "his sons".

anchors.fact: Cameron's Kick, a sour of scotch and Irish whiskey with lemon and orgeat, first appeared in his 1922 *ABC of Mixing Cocktails* (Oxford). His 1927 book prints it as one third each whisky and one sixth each lemon juice and orgeat. In 1922 he was "Harry of Ciro's", not yet at the Paris bar. (F12, F18)
anchors.meaning: Two countries' whiskies in one glass, on his own page. Ours changes it, and v2 owns that in words ("a little more lemon than his 1927 book does, and a touch more almond"). Only the 1927 proportions are known to us, so it's "his 1927 book". "First appeared in his book", never "his invention" or "his Paris bar's drink" for 1922.

anchors.fact: Sambuca is usually served "con la mosca", with coffee beans that with a little imagination look like houseflies. Oxford gives "one or three". (Oxford pdf 1723)
anchors.meaning: A borrowing, owned in one clause: "the way sambuca is often served". **Never "old" and never "an Italian way":** Oxford contrasts Rome's frozen sip with the fly served "around the world" (F26, D7). No luck lore.

anchors.fact: Roasted coffee beans are lighter than water: 438–755 kg/m³ against 1,000 (Rodrigues et al. 2003, Table 2). (F23)
anchors.meaning: That they float is our inference from the measured density, labelled ours. Never "never sink".

anchors.fact: Oxford's Espresso Martini is garnished with three coffee beans (pdf 739). (F25)
anchors.meaning: A look-alike to own in Checks. The image stays pale and never reads as an Espresso Martini.

cocktail.closingLine: Three flies, every time. If you ever stop, start again at three.
method: Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes.
Pour the scotch, the Irish whiskey, the lemon juice and the orgeat (the almond syrup) into a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds.
Strain it into the cold coupe.
Drop three coffee beans onto the middle of the drink. They float on the thin froth the shaking leaves. They're there for the eye and the nose. Bite one if you like.
cocktail.name: For Kicks

recipe.note: and another, half and half, the way Harry's book has it
a little more than his book's sixth, which leaves the drink short of sour
his book's own note says it's made from almonds
the fly: floated on top, never stirred in

cocktail.tagline: You take a joke further than anyone, until everyone else is in on it.

reading.epigraph: Three coffee beans float on top. They're meant to be flies. It's a long story.
whoYouAre: Somebody once said something daft in passing, and you didn't let it go. You took it one step further, then another. Now there's a word people use without knowing it started with you, a thing you always wear, a little ritual nobody remembers agreeing to. It started as a joke, and it's still a joke. You just never saw a reason to stop.

At every age, someone has expected you to grow out of it. What you don't say is that you could. Normal isn't a mystery to you: you could do it tomorrow, and nobody would stop you. That's the part that frightens you, more than any look across a room: how quietly it could happen. Meanwhile, next to you, other people get to be a bit ridiculous too, and they are. They feel freer around you than they'd ever think to tell you. That's a bigger gift than being taken seriously.
yours: The way a Paris bar's own book tells it, it started in 1924 with a gloomy piece by a New York columnist, who called the regulars of the Paris bars barflies: the ones who never seem to leave. His name, and this is true, was Oscar Odd McIntyre. Then a nightclub owner joked about it in an advert: his Christmas Eve takings would go to the "needy barflies".

Harry McElhone, a Scot who ran that bar, Harry's New York Bar, answered with an advert of his own, calling a meeting, and around Christmas the International Bar Flies was founded there. The book lists McIntyre as president, "Big Blue Bottlefly", and Harry as "Little Blue Bottlefly". By 1927 it had over five thousand members, and branches, called traps, from Shanghai to Buenos Aires. My guess is they joined for the reason people join in with you: someone had gone first, and was clearly fine.

The joke wasn't his. He just wouldn't let it end where most people would have, which is exactly what you do with a joke. And he kept it going. In 1940, as the war closed in, he locked his papers in a safe, buried it and left. After the war he returned to the bar and picked up where he left off, and a later booklet lists him as the society's president: "Exalted Blue Bottle Fly". He'd been promoted. I like to think the silliness was one of the things he kept safe.

The cocktail I've made for you is my take on Cameron's Kick, a forgotten classic, a whisky sour that first appeared in Harry's 1922 book. It's half Scotch whisky and half Irish whiskey, shaken with lemon and orgeat, a sweet almond syrup. Two countries' whiskies in one glass sounds like it shouldn't work, and it plainly does. I've given it a little more lemon than the old printed recipe, and a touch more almond, so it tastes brighter. Then I added the flies: three coffee beans floated on top, the way sambuca, an anise liqueur, is often served "with the fly", because with a little imagination the beans look like houseflies. Here they're for the Bar Flies. They add a little roasted-coffee scent as the glass comes up, and if you bite one, a bitter crunch against the almond.

Some stretches of your life will need you to be serious, and when one comes, you'll manage it. It doesn't get to take the silliness with it. When it's over, pick up where you left off: the word, the ritual, the thing you always wear, all of it. You won't be the only one who missed it.
